title: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Patch
summary: Defines a JSON document structure for describing a sequence of operations to apply to a JSON document, suited for the HTTP PATCH method. It uses the application/json-patch+json media type.

plainLanguage.summary: Rather than rewriting a whole page, you hand in a list of small edits: change this word, add that line, remove this one.

questions: how to update part of a json document with http patch
how does http patch use json patch
what operations does json patch support
what is the json patch media type
subtitle: A list of small edit instructions for changing part of a JSON document, built for HTTP PATCH.

tldr.problem: Sending a whole JSON document back just to change one value is wasteful, and HTTP PATCH needs some agreed format for describing a partial change.
tldr.mechanism: A JSON Patch document is a JSON array of operation objects (add, remove, replace, move, copy, test), each pointing at a location with a JSON Pointer. They are applied in order to the target document.
tldr.outcome: A patch is all-or-nothing when carried by HTTP PATCH, and a failed operation means the patch as a whole is not successful. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Operations
facts.value: add, remove, replace, move, copy, test

today: RFC 6902 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It relies on RFC 6901 for pointers and on RFC 5789 for the HTTP PATCH method.

sections.title: Why a Patch Format
sections.content:
JSON is a common format for exchanging and storing structured data, and the HTTP PATCH method (RFC 5789) lets a client make partial modifications to a resource. JSON Patch is the format, identified by the media type application/json-patch+json, for expressing a sequence of operations to apply to a target JSON document.

The RFC says the format is suitable for HTTP PATCH, but it is also useful wherever a partial update is needed for a JSON document or for a data structure that can be serialized as a JSON object or array.
sections.plainLanguage: If you only want to fix one typo in a long letter, you do not mail the whole letter again. You send a note saying which word to change.

sections.title: The Shape of a Patch Document
sections.content:
A JSON Patch document is itself a JSON document: an array of objects, where each object is one operation. Operations are applied sequentially in the order they appear. Each operation is applied to the target document, and the result becomes the target of the next operation. Evaluation continues until every operation has succeeded or an error is hit.

Every operation object MUST have exactly one op member, which is one of add, remove, replace, move, copy or test; any other value is an error. It MUST also have exactly one path member, a JSON Pointer string (RFC 6901) naming the target location. Other members depend on the operation, and members that an operation does not define MUST be ignored. The order of members inside an object does not matter.
sections.plainLanguage: A patch is a numbered checklist. Each line says what to do and where to do it. You work down the list from top to bottom, and each step sees the result of the one before.

sections.title: The Six Operations
sections.content:
add needs a value. If the target is an array index, the value is inserted there and later elements shift right; the index MUST NOT be greater than the number of elements, and an index of a single dash character appends to the end. If the target is an object member that does not exist, it is added; if it exists, its value is replaced. The parent object or array must already exist, so adding /a/b works when a exists but is an error when it does not.

remove deletes the value at the target, which MUST exist; later array elements shift left. replace needs a value and the target MUST exist; it is the same as a remove followed by an add at the same place.

move and copy take a from pointer that MUST exist. Move is a remove at from followed by an add at path; copy is an add at path using the value found at from. For move, the from location MUST NOT be a proper prefix of path, so a value cannot be moved into one of its own children.

test needs a value and succeeds only if the value at the target is equal to it.
sections.plainLanguage: You have six tools: put something in, take something out, swap something, move it, photocopy it, or check that it says what you expect before going on.

sections.title: When Two Values Are Equal
sections.content:
The test operation needs a precise idea of equality. Two values are equal only if they have the same JSON type and are equal by the rules for that type:

  • Strings: the same number of Unicode characters and byte-by-byte equal code points.
  • Numbers: numerically equal.
  • Arrays: the same number of values, each equal to the value at the same position in the other array.
  • Objects: the same number of members, with matching keys (compared as strings) and equal values.
  • Literals (false, true, null): the same literal.

The comparison is logical, so whitespace and the order of object members do not matter. The appendix shows that testing the number 10 against the string "10" fails.
sections.plainLanguage: To check two things match, they have to be the same kind of thing and say the same thing. The number 10 and the word "10" look alike but do not count as the same.

sections.title: Errors and All-or-Nothing
sections.content:
If a patch breaks a normative requirement, or an operation does not succeed, evaluation SHOULD stop and the application of the entire patch SHALL NOT be deemed successful. For status codes when used with HTTP PATCH, the RFC points to Section 2.2 of RFC 5789.

HTTP PATCH is atomic, so a patch that first replaces /a/b/c with 42 and then runs a failing test on it leaves the document completely unchanged. This makes test useful as a guard at the start of a patch.

An object with a duplicated member name, such as two op members, cannot be treated as a valid operation, because JSON has no standard error handling for duplicates.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a recipe where one bad step ruins the dish, so you throw the whole thing out and put everything back the way it was.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
JSON Patch has the same security considerations as JSON and JSON Pointer. The RFC adds one specific warning: a few older web browsers can be coerced into loading an arbitrary JSON document whose root is an array, which could expose a patch document containing sensitive information to attackers through a Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attack, even if access is authenticated.

The text estimates those browsers were used in less than 1% of the market at the time of writing. Publishers who are still concerned are advised to avoid making such documents available with HTTP GET.
sections.plainLanguage: Some very old browsers could be tricked into handing over a private list of edits. If that worries you, do not let people fetch the list by just asking for it.

viz.caption: THE SIX OPERATIONS AND WHAT EACH NEEDS (RFC 6902)

items.label: add
items.desc: Needs value. Inserts into an array, adds a member, or replaces an existing member.

items.label: remove
items.desc: Deletes the value at path, which must exist.

items.label: replace
items.desc: Needs value. Replaces the value at path, which must exist.

items.label: move
items.desc: Needs from. Removes at from, then adds at path.

items.label: copy
items.desc: Needs from. Adds at path a copy of the value at from.

items.label: test
items.desc: Needs value. Succeeds only if the value at path is equal.
